The underlying theme of Professor Swan￾son's current research in vibrational spec￾troscopy is to learn more about equilibrium
structure and reaction pathways by under￾standing the molecular vibrations of
molecules and crystals in their equilibrium
configurations. Molecular vibrations are di￾rect manifestations of the interatomic forces
in a molecule. From a knowledge of the
fundamental frequencies of vibration, and
other auxilliary vibrational data, one can hope
to define a potential energy function which is
related to the bonding forces in a molecule.
The tie between molecular vibrations and
reaction paths is a relatively new develop￾ment. In effect, one can hope to learn
something of dissociative pathways directly
from equilibrium properties of the reactant
molecule. Ultimately, this is the sort of infor￾mation which is needed before we can hope
selectively to effect a chemical reaction using
the least amount of energy, one of the major
goals of the emerging area of laser chemistry.
Professor Swanson is best known for his
structural and vibrational work on transition
metal complexes containing CO, CN', and
NO. These compounds are interesting from a
bonding standpoint by virtue of the possibility
of M-»L dir- prr* interactions in addition to
the usual M-*L sigma interaction. The cataly￾tic properties of metal carbonyls are a direct
result of the ability of CO to stabilize metals in
low valence states. Much of Swanson's early
work represents an effort to characterize the
trends in M-L® - andrr-bonding as a function
of the metal, its oxidation state, and its
coordinative environment.
The bonding and vibrational studies of
transition metal cyanides are being extended
to polynuclear cyanide complexes such as
Prussian blue and its analogs. These mater￾ials exhibit unusual properties. They act as
semipermeable membranes to the transport
of small H-bonding molecules. The polynu￾clear cyanides are also important from the
standpoint mixed valence chemistry. The
Fe'*2 and Fe*’ ions in Prussian blue, FeV [-
Fe'*'2(CN)(,]2 . XH2O, are separated by a linear
CN- bridge; Fe(ll) -C-N-Fe(lll). The two dif￾ferent metals interact with one another
through the rr* level on the CN“ ion, giving
rise to a facile electron transfer between iron
atoms. This valence delocalization is respon￾sible for the semiconductor properties of
Prussian blue complexes. Swanson's current
research on polynuclear cyanides is aimed at
optimizing the infervalence transfer by
changing the metals, their oxidation states,
and their coordinative environment.
The simple transition metal hexacyanides
such as Cs2LiFe(CN)6 exhibit structural phase
transformations as a function of temperature.
It has been possible to describe these phase

the crystal in the high temperature form.
Several of these salts exhibit second order

mode of vibration. Phase transitions of this

If has long been known that six transitional
metals - Mn, Fe, Co, Cu, Zn, and Mo - are
essential to vital processes in man and other
animals; these are commonly referred to as
•'the metals of life," or simply the "essential
metals." Further, the molecular structures of
hallucinogenic drugs such as heroin, mari￾huana, and mescaline are also well known
and if is recognized that such drugs produce
physiological effects that are both different
and characteristic.
An examination of the structures of the
hallucinogens suggests that all of them
should interact with the ions of the essential
metals to form coordination complexes, but
until the inception of the present research
program, this has remained a totally unex￾plored area. Its importance resides in the
possibility that if such complexes are formed
and are either extremely stable, very insolu￾ble owing (for example) to polymer formation,
or incapable of transport across membrane
structures, they could thereby deprive the
organism - partially or completely - of its
supply of these essential metals and thus be
involved in the mechanism of the physiologi￾cal activity of the drugs.
In its broadest outline, this program in￾volves two phases: (1) The in vitro synthesis,
characterization, and determination of struc￾ture (where feasible) of all possible coordina￾tion complexes that can be formed by the
hallucinogens and the essential metal; (2)
The in vivo comparison of the physiological
effects of these coordination complexes with
those of the parent drugs.
Although this work has been in progress
for only about two years, substantial progress
has already been made. The existence of
coordination compounds of marihuana in
solution has been demonstrated but their
isolation in pure crystalline form has not yet
been accomplished. With both mescaline and
heroin, however, several coordination com￾plexes have been isolated, purified, and fully
characterized. In the case of the structurally
related drug, d,l-methamphefamine, three

single crystal X-ray techniques.
The first in vivo experiments have been
initiated very recently, using white rats as the
exherimental animals. The first set of experi￾ments is designed to detect teratogenic ef￾fects of heroin and a copper complex of
heroin in female white rats in their second
week of pregnancy. Teratogeny (i.e., the gen￾eration of foetal monsters) was selected as an
experimental criterion because of its known
ease of detection and because if has been
postulated as one of the results of heroin
addition in pregnant humans. Since these are
as of now only exploratory and incomplete
studies, it is not yet possible to report any
definitive findings.

Professor Gilbert and his research group are
primarily interested in investigating thermally
and photochemically promoted reactions of
hydrocarbons. The goals of such research

such "hot” molecules. Furthermore, our

orbital symmetry in molecular rearrange￾ments.
The substrates we have investigated thus
far are small-ring hydrocarbons containing at
least one strategically located carbon-carbon
double bond, whose function is twofold, to
serve as a chromophore for the photochemi￾cal studies and to decrease the energy of
activation required tor initiation of reactions
by cleavage of a carbon-carbon single bond.
The combination of the considerable strain
inherent in small rings and the stabilizing
effect that double bonds have on radical-like
species has allowed thorough study of ther￾mal rearrangements occurring at tempera￾tures as low as 60°, a fact that greatly
simplifies finding answers to a variety of
mechanistic questions. Thus far several im￾portant hypotheses have been supported by
our investigations, among which is that com￾petitive sigmatropic processes occur at rates
that are a function of the relative energies of
the molecular orbitals involved in the
reactions.
Investigations are in progress to assess the
relationships, if any, between reactions oc￾curring on two distinctly different energy
surfaces; the electronic ground and excited
states. Thus, the fates of thermally and
photochemically activated substrates are
being compared and contrasted. Such
studies should allow definition of the various
energy surfaces and the possible interactions
between them. Although it has previously
been possible in only a few cases to make a
thorough comparison of the chemistry of
organic molecules in more than one electron￾ic state, we have developed approaches that
permit such studies to be performed on
molecules in three different electronic states.
Another program of research in Gilbert's
group involves the study of novel carbenes.
Of current interest in this area are the chemi￾cal and electronic properties of alkylidene￾carbenes produced by phofofragmentation.

The principal interests of Professor Pettit lie
in the field of organometallic chemistry
which, until recently, was a relatively unex￾plored area lying between the more conven￾tional fields of inorganic and organic
chemistry. Stabilization of normally reactive
organic molecules such as carbene and
cyclobutadiene is found to occur upon coor￾dination of these species to certain transition
metals; conversely, the activation of stable
organic species upon coordination to a metal
is the basis for catalysis in many instances.
The research area covers the study of
novel organometallic species, their potential
use in organic synthesis, and the mechanism
of organometallic reactions especially as ap￾plied to homogeneous and heterogeneous
catalysis. Of particular interest in the area of
homogeneous catalysis is the design of or￾ganometallic compounds which will be able
to effect chemical reduction utilizing carbon
monoxide and water in place of hydrogen.

Physical Chemistry and Chemical Physics
Graduate students interested in physical chemistry will find among fifteen
research groups at Texas a diversity of experimental and theoretical problems
from which to choose a research field. Several of these research groups span
more than one area.
Each of the experimental groups maintains its own laboratory facilities; in
addition the department maintains a strong group of major instruments
including mass, Raman, infrared, ultraviolet, nuclear magnetic resonance and
electron spin resonance spectrometers. The experimental research is also
supported by the glassblowing, electronics, and machine shops. The ten staff
members in these shops handle much of the construction and maintenance of
laboratory apparatus. The University computation center is used heavily in the
physical chemistry research done at Texas. This facility is accessible through
remote terminals throughout the chemistry building and. for batch process￾ing. at the satellite computer center terminal also located in the building.

Ph.D. Program of Study The general requirements of grade point and
course registration are those detailed for all chemistry students in the
graduate catalog. The particular requirements for a physical chemistry or
chemical physics degree are outlined below.
Entering students in physical chemistry are advised, on the basis of
entrance exams in physical chemistry, whether remedial work in this area
should be included as a part of their programs. Generally speaking, students
will be advised to begin work in physical chemistry without remedial study by
taking one of the two qualifying courses-statistical thermodynamics and
quantum chemistry. Students taking degrees in physical chemistry must take
both of these and qualifying courses in two other areas of chemistry-organic,
inorganic, analytical, or biochemistry. Students taking degrees in chemical
physics are required to take a qualifying course in one other area of chemistry
and, from an approved list, twelve hours from physics and mathematics.
During the latter part of their first semester or early part of the second
semester students are expected to select a research supervisor. Course work,
other than that described above, is to a large measure decided by the student,
the supervising professor, and a committee appointed by the graduate deain.

In selecting a supervisor, students are encouraged to interview all of the
faculty in physical chemistry as a means of informing themselves of the kinds
of subjects being investigated in the department.
During their third semester, students in physical chemistry and chemical
physics are required to prepare and defend orally three research proposals
on topics in physical chemistry of their own choosing, subject to the
restriction that the proposals must be from diverse areas of physical
chemistry. Satisfactory completion of a language requirement, as outlined in
the graduate catalog, is also expected within the first three semesters.
The division of physical chemistry, in cooperation with the analytical and
inorganic divisions, maintains a regular seminar program attended by both
students and faculty. The presentations, by department members and other
experts from around the world, offer students an opportunity to gain exposure
to progress in a number of different research areas.
The final requirements for the Ph D. degree are completion of the
dissertation research and an oral defense of this research before the
supervisory committee.

James Ernest Boggs
The research group working with Professor
Boggs is involved in the study of molecular
structure and dynamics. Both experimental
and theoretical methods are used, and an
attempt is made to combine and correlate the
two approaches. Most of the effort is con￾cerned with isolated molecules since the
interest is in the nature of intramolecular
forces rather than in crystal or solvent effects.
One major focus of the work of this group
is in the investigation of molecular conforma￾tions. Internal rotation of one part of a
molecule with respect to another can lead to
alternative stable structures which may or
may not be equivalent to each other.
Microwave spectroscopy has proved to be a
powerful tool in the investigation of such
systems, and it is a major technique used by
this group. In favorable cases, analysis of the
microwave spectrum leads to the identifica￾tion of the coexisting conformers, gives the
important details of their geometry with high
precision, determines their relative abun￾dance and difference in energy, measures
the spacings between vibrational levels of the
various forms and the corresponding funda￾mental vibrational frequencies, and finds the
energy barriers to internal rotation, inversion,
or ring puckering separating the conformers.
Although microwave spectroscopy can often
solve conformational problems alone, the
group has often found it useful to supplement
the microwave results with studies using in￾frared and Raman spectroscopy and with gas
phase electron diffraction.
Professor Boggs and his students are also
making important contributions to the investi￾gation of molecular structure by means of ab
initio molecular orbital calculations. Suffi￾cient experience is now available with the
determination within the Hartree-Fock ap￾proximation of energy-optimized geometries
of simple molecules (up to half a dozen
second-period atoms plus hydrogen) to per￾mit the technique to be comparable with
experimental methods in the following sense:
(1) It is well understood which structural
questions can be answered by this method
and which cannot. (2) For various cases,
there is a very high probability that the para￾meters will be reliable within known accura￾cies. An experiment can promise nothing
more. Use of computations is indicated in
cases where instability or other properties of
the substance make experimental study im￾possible or render the experimental results
unusually uncertain or less than normally
precise. Computation can investigate directly
the geometry of transition states or other
molecular conformations which are not at
minima on the potential energy surface, while
such geometries can be arrived at only very
indirectly if at all by experiment. The con￾struction of models to "explain” molecular
structures is greatly facilitated by examina￾tion of the way in which a structure responds
to artificial deformations applied by imposing
restraints in the geometry optimization. A
recent example of this is the study by the
group of Professor Boggs of the tilt and
asymmetry of methyl groups in asymmetric
environments
Another major research interest of the
group working with Professor Boggs deals
with the mechanism of transfer of rotational
energy during bimolecular collisions A
number of experimental studies have been
made by the group, but the major advances
have resulted from theoretical investigations
that have given clearer insight into the
process. Contributions have been made both
to the understanding of the role of long-range
intermolecular forces in weak collisions and
to the explanation of the molecular behavior
in close or strong collisions. The goal is to be
able to predict collisional transition probabili￾ties from fundamental molecular properties.
Professor Boggs is Director of the Center
for Structural Studies, a loose association of
the research groups at The University of
Texas at Austin who have common interests
in the study of the structure and dynamics of
isolated molecules. The Center promotes
cooperation among these groups by means of
joint seminars, frequent discussions, and joint
support of certain ventures. If also coordi￾nates a variety of collaborative research
programs with other institutions, particularly
in Germany, Norway, Hungary, and India. An
important international conference is spon￾sored in Austin in alternate years.
Professor Boggs is also an enthusiastic
classroom teacher. At various times he has
taught most of the courses in physical
chemistry, quantum mechanics, and molecu￾lar structure offered by the department as
well as making major contributions to the
teaching of freshman chemistry.

Professor Davis’ research interests lie in the
experimental study of molecular structure by
physical methods, especially X-ray crystallog￾raphy. A major thrust of his recent research

Examples of this research are seen in the

Similarly, many difficult organic reactions are

Research in this group is expanding in the

A continuing program is also underway

Denis Atan Kohl
Professor Kohl’s research area is the study of
gas-phase chemical reactions by electron
diffraction and mass spectrometry. The goal
of this research is the direct identification of
short-lived intermediates in chemical reac￾tions. Recent studies include the bromination
of ethylene and the structural isomerization of
cyclopropane to propylene. The radical addi￾tion of bromine to olefins is known to be
sterospecific with trans-only addition to dou￾ble bonds. An electron diffraction study of
this reaction showed that the first bromine
forms a symmetric bridge across the double
bond with significant double bond character
to each of the carbon-bromine bonds. This
rigid three-membered ring prevents rotation
about the carbon-carbon bond and accounts
for the trans-only addition. The study of the
rearrangement of cyclopropane indicated
that the reaction proceeds through a highly
distorted three-membered ring. Current work
is devoted to extending knowledge about
reaction intermediates, and involves study of
laser-induced reactions.

Robert Eugene Wyatt
Professor Wyatt and his group are carrying
out theoretical studies of chemical reaction
dynamics within both the classical and quan￾tal formulations of scattering theory. These
studies aim to provide a detailed molecular
level description of energy transfer in chemi￾cal reactions.
Although extensive classical and statistical
results on reaction dynamics have been ob￾tained over the past fifteen years, very few
quantum results are available Part of the
problem is the enormous scale of the compu￾tations, but the preliminary mathematical an￾alysis of the Schrodinger equation for the
reaction is far from trivial. Because of these
difficulties of treating reactions in full three￾dimensional space, much effort since 1969
has been devoted to accurate studies of
atom-molecule reactions for dimensionally
restricted collinear and coplanar geometries.
Over the past several years, we have devel￾oped techniques for treating three￾dimensional reactive collisions through use
of special sets of curvilinear coordinates
which blend smoothly from a set most suita￾ble for reactants to a set most suitable for
products. The Hamiltonian operator in these
"natural coordinates" is then decomposed
into translational, vibrational, and rotational
components. The rotational Hamiltonian is
that of an asymmetric top with a hindered
internal degree of freedom (the hindering
results from the tendency to form a transition
state with a preferred geometry). Because of
this Hamiltonian decomposition, the scatter￾ing wavefunction can be expanded in
products of vibrational and asymmetric top
wavefunctions, with expansion coefficients
which are found by numerical solution of a
system of coupled second-order differential
equations. From the expansion coefficients
(translational wavefunctions), elements of the
scattering matrix (S-matrix) can be extracted,
from which reaction probabilities and cross
sections for specific processes can be
computed.
The three-dimensional H -t- H? and F 4 H2
reactions have been extensively studied with
this formalism. Specific new results have
been obtained on the following topics: energy
dependence of cross sections leading to
specific product vibration-rotation states, an￾gular momentum partitioning in the products,
average geometry and energy partitioning in
the reaction intermediates, factors determin￾ing shapes of reaction probabilities near
threshold, and probability and flux distribu￾tions near resonance energies. In addition to
these accurate quantum studies of specific
reactions, approximate quantum and classi￾cal mechanical methods are being studied,
the aim of which is the fast and reasonably
accurate production of reaction probabilities.

Entrance and Degree Requirements
Master of Arts The Master of Arts degree is based upon satisfactory
completion of thirty semester hours of work, of which the thesis counts for six
semester hours. From six to twelve hours of the course work must be taken in
an outside but closely allied graduate area (usually mathematics, physics,
biological sciences, geological sciences, pharmacy, or chemical engineering,
but occasionally others, such as education). Up to nine hours of work of
upper division rank, but not more than six hours in either the major or the
minor, may be counted in the program; the balance must be in courses of
graduate rank. The submission of a thesis based upon independent scientific
research is an integral component of this degree.
Doctor of Philosophy Many graduate students in chemistry work directly
toward the Ph.D. degree without the M.A. degree as an intermediate objective.
Advanced course work is an integral part of the doctoral candidate’s program;
however, there is no set minimum number of semester hours required for the
degree. The Ph.D. degree is awarded on the basis of the candidate’s
demonstration of mastery of the selected field and of his/her ability for
independent scholarship in it. In addition to the major area representing the
most intensive field of study, the candidate will take ’’supporting work” to
broaden or supplement the field of specialization; the supporting work may be
outside of the major department.
The preliminary training of students wishing to major in chemistry for a
oraduate degree must include a minimum of twenty-four semester hours in
chemistry, of which twelve or more must be of at least upper-division (junior
and senior level) courses. Within the twenty-four hours, there should have
been two semester courses (including laboratory) in organic chemistry and
two in physical chemistry; one in analytical chemistry; and one in inorganic
chemistry. Applicants lacking the prescribed background may still be admit￾ted, but will be required to satisfy any such deficiencies with appropriate
coursework.
For entrance into the Graduate School, an applicant must
(1) hold a bachelor’s degree from an accredited institution in the U.S. or
have had equivalent training in a foreign university;
(2) have a B average in upper division work and any graduate work already
completed;
(3) score at least 1000 on the Graduate Record Examination Aptitude Test.
In addition, the admissions committee of the Department of Chemistry
strongly recommends, but does not require, that applicants submit scores
from the Advanced Chemistry Test of the Graduate Record Examination.
The chemistry faculty believes that teaching experience is an essential part
of the education of graduate students, and therefore requires each degree
candidate to teach, usually by taking charge of laboratory work in undergra￾duate courses, for a minimum of two semesters. The Graduate School
recognizes the value of this experience by awarding three semester hours of
credit (which may be applied toward a graduate degree) for a minimum of two
semesters of registration in Chemistry 398T, Supervised Teaching for
Graduate Students.
82
Qualification for candidacy for the Ph.D. degree is attained by:
(1) Meeting the Graduate School requirement of proficiency in one foreign
language. In chemistry, any of the languages of chemical science; German is
strongly recommended for organic chemists. The foreign language require￾ment can be satisfied by (a) completion of twelve semester hours of study of
the language at an accredited institution with an average of at least B; (b) by
passing an examination approved by the Dean; or (c) by passing a language
course specifically designed to fulfill the reading ability requirement.
(2) Satisfactory completion of courses (or, at the student’s option, by taking
examinations) chosen from those specified as qualifying courses, in three of
the five principal areas of graduate work in the department: analytical,
biochemical, inorganic, organic, and physical. A student must qualify in the
field of his or her major interest. In some cases, the major division or the
supervising professor may recommend the areas for qualification. A student
may qualify in chemical physics by taking the courses (or examinations) in
physical chemistry and one other field in chemistry, plus specified courses in
physics and mathematics. Students who enter with graduate credit from
another university for courses essentially equivalent to the qualifying courses
may qualify for Ph.D. candidacy either by passing an examination in the
qualifying course of by completing a more advanced course in the same area.
A student is expected to meet the foreign language requirement, complete
successfully (with a grade of at least B) the required qualifying courses (or
examinations), and select a research supervisor within twelve months after
entering Graduate School.
After admission to candidacy, the student’s program of work is under the
direction of a supervising committee, the head of which is the research
supervisor. The supervising committee tests the candidate’s mastery of the
major field (major examination), passes on the quality of the dissertation, and
conducts the final oral examination (defense of the dissertation).
83
Financial Support
Most qraduate students in chemistry receive financial support in the form of
assistantships or fellowships. As noted earlier, some teaching experience is
reouired of all candidates for a graduate degree in chemistry. About eighty
Teaching Assistantships and Assistant Instructorships are awarded each
year, primarily for teaching students in undergraduate laboratory courses^
These appointments usually require six to eight contact hours per week of
laboratory teaching, and some additional time for student conferences,
qrading, etc. A teaching assistant typically registers for ten to twelve semester
hours of credit, of which up to six would be in formal coursework.
Appointments are based upon the applicant’s grade record in undergraduate
and any previous graduate work, letters of recommendation, general promise
of successful pursuit of graduate study, and acceptance for admission to the
Graduate School. Stipends range upward from $3700 (depending on quaUfi￾cations of the applicant and on performance as a Teaching Assistant) for nine
months. Summer Teaching Assistantships and various fellowships are availa￾ble for Summer Sessions. A teaching assistant who is not a resident of Texas
nevertheless pays only the resident tuition for the course load taken (ten
semester hours minimum). Prospective graduate students should apply for a
Teaching Assistantship by writing to the Chairman, Department of Chemistry,
The University of Texas, Austin, Texas 78712.
University and other fellowships are also awarded to outstanding applicants
for graduate appointments. In addition to substantial stipends, many of these
appointments carry supplements for payment of tuition and required fees, and
in some cases an allowance for dependents. Application forms for these
fellowships may be obtained from the Director of Fellowships, Graduate
School, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, or from the
Chairman of the Department of Chemistry.
Research Assistantships financed by contracts or grants to faculty mem￾bers are available to and the most important source of support for graduate
students. Appointments to these positions are made directly by the faculty
member holding the grant, and are usually available after the student has
been in graduate school for about a year. Most graduate students who have
held a teaching assistantship for a year or more later transfer to a research
assistantship for the latter part of their work.
84
Miscellaneous Information
The University of Texas at Austin operates on the semester system, with the
Fall semeser usually beginning about August 25 and the Spring semester
about January 15. Summer school consists of two six-week terms, although
some courses are taught over a period of nine or twelve weeks. A graduate
student normally fulfills the coursework requirements of the Department and
Graduate School by taking three to six formal semester hours of classes for
four semesters. Thus, entering graduate students in chemistry register for
thirteen semester hours for each of the first two semesters, of which seven
hours are normally for supervised teaching and the entering graduate student
seminar and six are formal courses.
Registration Expenses: The total costs for tuition and required fees, including
the fee for use of the Student Health Center, each semester are
approximately:
10 semester hours 12 semester hours
Texas residents $160 $176
U.S. citizens 510 606
Foreign students 510 606
Teaching assistants and fellowship holders qualify for resident tuition; thus
virtually no chemistry graduate students at the University of Texas pay the
higher rates.
Employment for Spouses: Part-time and full-time positions are frequently
available on the campus for spouses of graduate students. The greatest
demand is for those with secretarial experience; there are also positions in the
various laboratories and libraries on the campus for those who are technically
trained. Employment opportunities are also provided by the city schools, by
many State and Federal government offices and agencies, and by private
industries located in Austin. A list of these offices, agencies, and industries
can be obtained from the Austin Chamber of Commerce, P. O. Box 1967,
Austin, Texas 78767.
Housing: The University provides a unit for single graduate students in
Jester Center, a modern dormitory on campus. The current rate for room
(double occupancy) and board (you must contract for both) is about $1544 for
the academic year. Single graduate students may also live in other University
residence halls, although Jester is the only place where an entire unit is
reserved for graduate students.
For married students, the University maintains a group of four apartment
complexes and a trailer park located about three miles from campus on the
Colorado River. Monthly rental for this housing ranges from $53 for a
two-bedroom unfurnished apartment at Brackenridge and Deep Eddy to $136
for a two-bedroom furnished apartment at Gateway. Trailer-park lots are $23
per month. The rent includes gas and water, but electricity is additional.
85
There sometimes is a waiting list for married student housing, so applies
tion for an apartment for the semester of your choice should be made as soon
as possible. For further information and application forms contact:
Division of Housing and Food Service
Box 7666
University Station
Austin, Texas 78712
Most graduate students stay in the private housing scattered throughout
Austin. Although the cost of such housing varies considerably, typically
rentals (not including electricity) are $150-$180 (one-bedroom) and $200-230
(two-bedroom) for unfurnished apartments; furnished apartments cost $15-20
more per month.
Entertainment: Entertainment in Austin is no problem. The University offers
to students who buy the "Activities Fee" (about $32 per year) a wide variety of
cultural and athletic events at little or no cost per event. Plays, concerts,
recitals, movies, and lectures by famous personalities are also sponsored by
the University and admission is often free. The City of Austin maintains a
varied recreational program with many parks and playgrounds. There are
excellent municipal swimming pools. Tennis courts and golf courses are
located about the city. Two lakes exist within the city limits, and six others are
scattered up and down the Colorado River within driving distance. There are
several civic play groups. Many excellent restaurants and numerous night
clubs for dancing and entertainment can be found in Austin.
Costs for off-campus activities cover a considerable range but prices
typically would be as follows: movies, $2-2.50; plays, $3-5; concerts, $3-6; and
restaurants, $2-7; nightclubs, $0-2 (cover charge), $1-1.50 (drinks).
Professional Employment: Degree holders from the Chemistry department
at UT-Austin enter the complete spectrum of positions available to profession￾al chemists. For example, of the individuals who completed their degrees
during the past five years, approximately 20% are currently in post-doctoral or
research scientist positions in academic or medical school settings, 28% hold
professorial appointments, and 35% are employed in industry. The remainder
are working in government-related laboratories and the like.
Graduates who wish to enter industrial positions are aided in their
job-hunting by the Engineering-Science Career Center, which provides a
central clearing-house for prospective employers and employees to make
contact. This center supplies advice about writing effective resumes, repro- /-
duces them at a nominal cost, and regularly posts announcements of
job-openings and interview schedules for many different companies that are
seeking chemists.
There are no geographical boundaries for our graduates in that they find
positions throughout the U.S. as well as abroad.
Fraternal Organizations: Chapters of Phi Lambda Upsilon (honorary chemi￾cal and chemical engineering fraternity) and Alpha Chi Sigma (professional
chemical and chemical engineering fraternity) are active at the University.
Members of any of these organizations will be glad to be of assistance to new
chemistry students; feel free to write to them if you plan to enter the
University. Inquiries directed to these organizations can be sent to them in
care of the Department of Chemistry.
86

Corals are important natural
resources that are key to the
ocean's vast biodiversit y and
provide economic, cultural, and
scientific benefit s. As a result
of human activities, locally and
globally, coral reefs are
declining rapidly. The
complexit y of corals makes
conserving and restoring reefs
very challenging. Corals are
made up of thousands of
different organisms, including
the animal host and the algae,
bacteria, viruses, and fungi that
coexist as a so-called
holobiont. Thus, corals are
more like cities than individual
animals, as they provide
factories, housing, restaurant s,
nurseries, and more for an
entire ecosystem.
Dr. Judith Klein-Seetharaman is
leading a two-year NSF project
that's bringing together
expert s in coral biology,
computer science, systems
biology, nanotoxicology and
structural engineering to
harness the data revolution in
biology with machine learning
to study how corals grow and
function, when viewed as if
they were manufacturing sites
in the ocean. Through there
remarkable abilities, corals can
'print' resources for themselves
and hundreds of thousands of
other species, just like a 3D
printer. The goal of this project
is to understand these
processes well enough to
control them in the lab.

Many believe that hydrogen fuel cells and
electrolyzers could be the key to creating
sustainable energy in the future. Electrolyzers can
utilize renewable energy to produce hydrogen for
subsequent use in either manufacturing processes,
or to run a fuel cell, generating electricit y on
demand. Despite significant investment s in these
promising technologies, cost and durabilit y are still
problematic, due to their reliance on expensive
catalyst s and the low manufacturing volumes of
electrolyzers and fuel cells component s.
Svitlana Pylypenko (Mines) and Jasna Jankovic
(UConn) are teaming with industry partners Pajarito
Powder and Forge Nano, the U.S Department of
Energy?s National Renewable Energy Laboratory,
and Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in
Germany to accelerate the development of
high-volume fabrication of component s to facilitate
the development of sustainable and zero-emission
energy generation technologies. The team will
compare the impact of various processes for
scale-up of electrolyzer and fuel cell electrodes on
electrode morphology and performance, based on
innovative and state-of-the-art catalyst s. With the
Partnership for Innovations grant from the National
Science Foundation, team will provide a common
platform for advanced and sophisticated
characterization for the developed product s and
establish process-properties-performance
correlations. This will make it possible for other
industrial partners to develop the tools and replicate
this process, which will further increase
commercialization of this technology. Due to the
collaborative nature of this project, student s will
have extensive technical, leadership, organizational,
communication, and entrepreneurial training. This
will help to prepare the student s as future leaders in
the clean energy sector. International workshops on
advanced manufacturing and characterization of
fuel cells and electrolyzers will help to expand
interactions with partners and form larger networks.

The Rocky Mountain Camp for Dyslexic youth
serves 40 student s every summer drawn
from across the country, ages 7-13, all who
have been diagnosed with the learning
disabilit y of dyslexia. Mines facult y and
student s from Chemistry, Materials Science,
and Chemical Engineering come together to
offer a STEM immersive experience each
summer. Specifically, we develop and
implement instructional hands-on modules,
based on STEM concept s. We have learned
through participating that the modules need
to be engaging, hands-on, and provide an
immediate feedback loop. Student s like camp
so much, that ~50 % of the student s attend
multiple years.
This outreach doesn?t stop with the summer
camp though. Once the modules have been
refined, based on what is learned during the
summer implementation, a Mines graduate
student will provide assistance to a Vertical
Skills Academy science teacher as they
implement these modules in the classroom.
Vertical Skills Academy is a specialized
dyslexia school with student s in grades 1-8 in
Evergreen, Colorado. Since the student s who
attend the camp do not have a dyslexic
school option in their communit y, the two
outreach activities serve different student
populations. The Rocky Mountain Camp for
Dyslexic youth offers opportunit y to
implement specific modules, while Vertical
Skills Academy offers the potential to further
refine and expand these modules and test
their impact during the academic year.
This effort is very important in bringing
student s who otherwise may have struggled
with school due to dyslexia an opportunit y to
show their interest and passion for STEM.
According to the International Dyslexia
Association approximately 10 percent of U.S.
school-age children and 40 million American
adult s (only about 2 million of the adult s
know it) have dyslexia. Although these
student s struggle to read, many display an
intense interest in (STEM). In fact, while
dyslexia may be disadvantageous for
professions that require repetition, many of
those diagnosed feel there are advantages
with regards to their perception, visualization
and creativit y.
Examples of scientist s that have overcome
dyslexia and made major impact include:
Thomas Edison, Michael Faraday, Alexander
Graham Bell, Albert Einstein, Nicola Tesla,
Steven Hawking and Louis Pasteur among
many, many others.
Chemistry department outreach to dyslexic youth
outreach
Potatoes from a different perspective
10 COLORADOSCHOOLOFMINES
At the Rocky Mountain Camp for Dyslexic
youth, student s are engaged in variet y of
experiment s created by Mines facult y and
student s. One is looking at potato catalase,
which is an enzyme found in potatoes that
catalytically decomposes hydrogen peroxide
to produce visible oxygen bubbles making it
an inexpensive, safe and effective hands on
tool for learning about enzymes.
Student s generally start forming hypotheses
very quickly about how it works by comparing
different sizes of pieces (surface area effect s),
cooking the potato (decomposing the
enzyme and not being able to regenerate),
freezing pieces of the potato (doesn?t work
frozen but activit y restored as it warms), etc.
The student s figure various aspect s of this
over 30-40 minutes with varying levels of
scientific insight s.
One particular girl, Serene (we checked and
she had not done this or heard about it
before) had done all of this in about 10
minutes. When asked what she had found, she
provided not only a detailed explanation of
how the enzyme works but also why a potato
would need to have the enzyme in the first
place and tied it back in with how peroxide
works to disinfect a cut on human skin
(noting that the skin doesn?t produce bubbles
but the cut/ infection does). Absolutely
amazed with her depth of insight and abilit y
to connect numerous observations. we later
discussed this with one of the lead counselors
who told us that this particular student
suffered so severely from dyslexia that she
had just begun to read sentences that
summer at the age of 11-years-old and was
unable recite the days of the week or months
of the year in order after weeks of working
on both.
Upon discussing further, she was from
Washington and her grandmother had rented
a motorhome and moved to Colorado for the
summer so Serene could attend the Rocky
Mountain Camp. While discussing the girl?s
numerous ?aha? moment s in science, her
grandmother commented that science was
her favorite part of the day and they talked
excitedly about the STEM activities they were
going to do throughout the year.
CHEMISTRY.MINES.EDU 11
For more info, read ?The Dyslexic Advantage?
by Eide and Eide Rocky Mountain Camp:
or visit rockymountaincamp.org
OUTREACH
Summer campers look to Mines chemistry student s for
real-world science inspiration
Student Stories
Michael Dzara, Materials Science (left) was one of three
student s to receive the Graduate Research Award at the 66th
International Meeting of the American Vacuum Societ y in
Columbus, Ohio.
This award recognizes excellence in graduate studies focused
on vacuum science and technology and related fields. At the
division level, Dzara was also recognized as a recipient of the
Applied Surface Science Division Student Award. He won these
awards based on his thesis work entitled "Characterization of
surface and interface properties of polymer electrolyte
membrane fuel cell catalyst s with X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy".
The Mines American Vacuum
Societ y (AVS) student
chapter had a successful year.
In addition to the normal
activities that make Mines AVS
one of the most active student
chapters in the societ y,
Chapter President Sarah
Zaccarine and member Natalie
Seit zman co-organized the

Catching up with Dr. Lin at Virginia Tech
Dr. Feng Lin,
currently an
assistant professor
of chemistry at
Virginia Tech,
graduated from
the Mines
Department of
Chemistry in 2012.
He was advised by
Professor Ryan
Richards and
worked on a
collaborative
smart windows project at National Renewable
Energy Laboratory. He took the facult y position
at Virginia Tech in Fall 2016 after his postdoc at
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and an
industry job in the Silicon Valley.
Dr. Lin's research group develops new
experimental methodologies and establish novel
design principles to enhance the electrochemical,
catalytic and optical properties of ion
intercalating solids for energy storage, chemical
conversion and electrochromics. Feng?s
academic career was nucleated at Mines, where
he was exposed to the multidisciplinary research
environment between Mines and NREL.
Feng resides in Christiansburg, Virginia with his
wife, Dr. Chixia Tian, who also graduated from
Mines' Chemistry Department and is a facult y
member at the Nanoscience Program at Virginia
Tech. Their days in Colorado taught them
everything about mountains and snow. Their
daughter Leyi Lyrica Lin was born in September
2019.
Before Mines, I remember applying for the
E-Days scholarship, a full ride to Mines based on
an essay about the wonderful places a Mines
degree will take you once you finish. I described
a fantastical future where my ?multidisciplinary
Mines degree? made me the ideal candidate for
a manned mission to Mars. Of course, I wasn?t
awarded the scholarship, but I still got that
multidisciplinary Mines degree and thankfully
learned to be a little less full of myself. Now, I
may not be on my way to Mars, but
coincidentally, my essay wasn?t as far from the
truth as one may think. After starting grad
school in chemistry at Stanford Universit y, I
joined the Waymouth lab and with it became
part of a NASA-funded project called CUBES
(Center for Utilization of Biological Engineering
in space) which is tasked with producing a
closed-loop ecosystem for the coming Mars
mission.
My project focuses on manufacturing tools and
other component s for when the astronaut s
need something that they forgot to pack. I work
with polyhydroxybut yrate (PHB) and other
copolymer polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) that
are produced as energy storage compounds for
Vince Pane: manufacturing tools for
astronaut s through an interdisciplinary scope
bacteria known as methanotrophs when they
eat methane and carbon dioxide. These
materials are ideally suited for closed-loop
resource utilization because a tool can be fed
right back to the bacteria to produce virgin
polymer. My work is the intersection of many
disciplines as I must figure out a method for
processing the bacteria+polymer into a usable
feedstock, 3D print the resulting material and
use polymer synthesis to inform the biologist s
of the best copolymers for 3D printing.
In my free time, I am working with inmates at
San Quentin State Penitentiary on
collaborative artworks. I am currently working
with Bruce Fowler (a long-time sculptor and
painter). We plan our art through letters and
prison visit s and really made a connection with
his long lost and my newfound love of the
ocean. In the pictured sculpture, I created the
wave from plastic collected on the beach,
while Fowler used floor wax, paint and other
prison-available materials for the surfer.
Vince Pane completed his B.S. Chemistry, May
2016 and M.S. in Mechanical Engineering, May
2017.

Phenylketonuria. The genetic disease
nylketonuria (PKU) is characterized by
1 levels in blood plasma of phenylalanine

enzymes are being used to construct extracor￾poreal shunt.s which will act in a manner

Professor Martin’s research interests focus on
the total synthesis of alkaloid and terpene
natural products which exhibit interesting
pharmacological properties. Although the
synthesis of the target molecules themselves is
often the primary objective of these studies, he
emphasizes the equally important task of
designing and developing general synthetic
methodology for the regio- and stereoselective
formation of new carbon-carbon bonds.
Frequently, selective procedures for the in￾troduction and manipulation of functional
groups in highly functionalized molecules must
be designed.
Recently, he completed the syntheses of
mesembrine and several related alkaloids
utilizing a versatile synthetic strategy which
represents a general entry to the related but
structurally more complex Amaryllidaceae
alkaloids. For example, he is presently working
toward the total syntheses of pretazettine, a
potent in vivo and in vitro antiviral and anti￾tumor agent, and galanthamine, a remarkably
effective analgesic and anticholinesterase
drug. In addition he has completed the
synthesis of the interesting spirosesquiterpene
acorone. Studies directed toward the synthesis
of other natural products which possess inter￾esting physiological properties and exhibit
potential medicinal utility are in progress.
Since the development of new synthetic
methodology is so crucial to the successful
synthesis of naturally occurring compounds.
Professor Martin is actively exploring a variety
of new synthetic procedures and strategies. In
particular, he is investigating new laboratory
procedures for the construction of quaternary
carbon centers by carbonyl homolo￾gation/alkylation operations which result in
the overall geminal alkylation at a carbonyl
carbon. He is also concerned with the design of
new reagents for effecting normal and modified
annelations. On another front, he has

homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis. Of
particular interest in the area of homogeneous
catalysis is the design of organometallic com￾pounds which will be able to effect chemical
reduction of utilizing carbon monoxide and
water in place of hydrogen.

The research group working with Professor
Boggs is involved in the study of molecular
structure and dynamics. Both experimental
and theoretical methods are used, and an
attempt is made to combine and correlate the
two approaches. Most of the effort is concerned
with isolated molecules, since the interest is in
the nature of chemical bonding and in￾tramolecular forces rather than in crystal or
solvent effects.
One major area of recent interest has been in
the ab initio computation of molecular struc￾tures. Professor Boggs and his coworkers have
developed new techniques that have made it
possible to compute forces acting on atoms
directly, making it feasible to determine
structures of molecules with 10-20 atoms at a
high level of reliability. Like various exper￾imental methods, the computational deter￾mination of molecular structure has certain
limitations, but there are also areas in which the
computed structures are more reliable thari
those that can be obtained by any experimental
technique. The group is interested in develop￾ing those areas of structural chemistry where
rapid and accurate answers to chemically
interesting problems can be obtained by this
method. Recent examples include studies of the
tilt and asymmetry of methyl groups in asym￾metric environments, the distortion of ring
systems due to interaction with substituents,
and the structure of metastable conformations
of molecules. In numerous uses, the computa￾tions have demonstrated errors in previous
experimental structural determinations.
A second important application of the new
computation tools is in the study of geometry
changes along the potential energy surfaces
corresponding to conformational changes.
Internal rotation and molecular inversion are
normally treated as one-coordinate problems
in experimental studies, simply because there
is no better alternative, but studies from the
group of Professor Boggs have given many
examples of the large magnitude of the defor￾mations in other molecular parameters during
the course of such internal conformational
changes. The computational methods can be
applied to transition slates or other inter￾mediate states in the course of such processes as
well as to the equilibrium states.
Still another application of the computa￾tional approach is to the more rigorous inter￾pretation of qualitative ideas of bonding. A
recent contribution from the group has given
new insight into the valence shell electron pair
repulsion model for the prediction of molecular
shape and bond angles. Other work has dealt
with such concepts as the significance of d
orbitals in bonds to silicon and sulfur.
On the experimental side, the group of
Professor Boggs has been involved for many
years in microwave spectroscopic determina￾tions of molecular structure and conformation.
Microwave spectroscopy has proved to be a
powerful tool in structural chemistry. In favor￾able cases, analysis of the microwave spec￾trum leads to the identification of coexisting
molecular conformers, gives the important
details of their geometry with high precision,
determines their relative abundance and dif￾ference in energy, measures the spacings
between vibrational levels of the various forms,
and finds the energy barriers to internal rota￾tion, inversion, or ring puckering separating the
stable conformers. Although microwave spec￾troscopy can often solve conformational
problems alone, the group has often found it
useful to supplement the microwave results
with studies using infrared and Raman spec￾troscopy, gas phase electron diffraction, or
computation.

Professor Davis’ research interests lie in the

William Cecil Gardiner, Jr.
The recent history of reaction kinetics has
shown that chemical reactions can be under￾stood with confidence over a wide spectrum of
levels of detail, ranging from the macroscopic
dissection of chemical changes into their
elementary molecular-level steps all the way to
quantum-mechanical descriptions of reactive
collisions between species in particular quan￾tum states. Research in our laboratory has
spanned roughly the top half of this spectrum,
concentrating on gas-phase reactions that are
amenable to detailed study and also of practical
interest outside the domain of pure chemistry.
At present the systems under study are
predominantly combustion reactions and
related pyrolytic reactions that occur in
homogeneousgas-phase combustion. Methane,
other small hydrocarbons, and the inter￾mediate species which participate in their
combustion are the fuels of interest. The ex￾periments are done by initiating reaction with
adiabatic compression of premixed test gases
in shock waves, the ensuing chemical reactions
being observed by means of kinetic absorption
and emission spectroscopy. Data interpretation
is done by means of computer simulation of the
reaction under the physical constraints ap￾propriate to the experiments. For the combus￾tion of very small fuel molecules such as H2 and
CO, experiments of this nature have proved
capable of defining the reaction mechanisms
and the relevant elementary reaction rate
constant expressions to such accuracy that the
course of their combustion processes can now
be simulated by computers over wide ranges of
conditions with equal or better accuracy than
most experiments. Whether the same goal can
be attained for hydrocarbon combustion with
similar techniques of reaction initiation but
more sophisticated techniques for following
the course of reaction will be discovered in
experiments now in progress in our laboratory
and elsewhere.

Primary photochemical process; non-radiative
processes in photochemistry; fluorescence and
phosphorescence.
The principal objective of the research in
Professor Noyes' laboratory is the detailed
elucidation of the photochemical primary
process, i.e., the determination of what happens
to molecules which absorb photons. The
processes include; (a) fluorescence; (b) dis￾sociation; (c) rearrangements; (d) crossover to
another state with a different number of paired
electron spins. At short wave lengths ionization
can result. Process (d), which usually causes
two spins that had been antiparallel to become
parallel, can be followed by phosphorescence
and any of the other processes. Detailed
balancing of all of these possibilities with the
number of photons absorbed provides the
fundamental basis for photochemistry.
Most of the recent work has centered around
aromatic compounds where the absorption is
due to the electrons in the aromatic ring. There
may be transfer of the absorbed energy to other
molecules on collision. If there are side chains,
the reactions may take place in the side chains
rather than in the aromatic ring itself. Some of
the most interesting reactions involve aromatic
molecules with unsaturated side chains and
molecules with cyclic side chains. Many dif￾ferent rearrangements are possible in such
cases.
One of the most difficult problems in this
type of study relates to the number of
molecules formed in the triplet excited state.
Present methods involve addition of a moni￾toring substance, but such an additive may
change the character of the primary process.
Attempts to devise better methodology are
being made.
Although Dr. Noyes is no longer supervising
graduate students, he and his postdoctoral
associates provide a valuable departmental
resource in their areas of expertise.

Miscellaneous Information
School Calendar:
The University of Texas at Austin operates on the semester system, with the Fall semester
usually beginning about August 25 and the Spring semester about January 15. Summer school
consists of two six-week terms, although some courses are taught over a period of nine or twelve
weeks.
Course Load:
A graduate student normally fulfills the coursework requirements of the Department and
Graduate School by taking three to six semester hours of formal, organized classes for four
semesters. First year graduate students in chemistry usually register for twelve semester hours for
each of the first three semesters, of which six hours are for supervised teaching and the entering
graduate student seminar and six are organized courses. In subsequent years, students register for
ten hours each semester of the academic year and for six hours during the summer.

are also entitled to resident tuition and fei^s.
Employment for Spouses.
Part-tinie and full-time positions <ir(! frequimtly a va liable on lh»; campus for spousi^s of graduate
Students-The greatest demand is for those with secretarial experience; there are also positions in
the various laboratories and libraries on the campus for those who are technically trained.
Employment opportunit ies are also provided by the city’s schools and hospitals, by the many State
and Federal government offices and agencies, and by the numerous private industries located in
Austin. A list of these offices, agencies, and industries can be obtained from the Austin t'.hamber
of Commerce, P. O. Box 1967, Austin, TX 7H7fj7.
Taxes;
Ther^ Ufe no local or state inc.ome t<ixes in 1 exas. 1 eaching and research assistantships are
generally subject to Federal taxation although fellowships are not. Because all graduate stud(;nts
are required to teach for one y<!ar, th(; IRS has established a policy of treating one y»;ar's worth of
income from a teaching assistantship as equivalent to a fellowship. Consequently, any money
withheld from the assistantship is refunded at the end of the tax year.
Both teaching and research assistantships are subject to social security lax. Howiiver, the State
of Texas presently pays not only its own but also thi; employee's portion of this, and the policy is
expected to be continued.
There is a limited 5% sales tax in Austin. Items such as food and prescription drugs are not
subject to this tax.
Housing:
The University provides a unit for single graduate students in Jester Center, a modern dormitory
on campus. The current rate for room (double occupancy) anti board (you must contract for both)
is about $1,820 for the academic year. Single graduate students may also live in other University
residence halls, although Jester is the only place whtire an entire unit is reserved for graduate
students.
For married students, the University maintains a group of four apartment complexes and a
trailer park located about three miles from campus on the Colorado River. Monthly rental for this
housing ranges from $86 for a two-bedroom unfurnished apartment at Brackenridge and Deep
Eddy to $150 for a two-bedroom furnished apartment at Gateway. Trailer-park lots are $30 per
month. The rent includes gas and water, but electricity is additional.
There sometimes is a waiting list for student housing, so application for a unit for the semester
of your choice should br; made as soon as possible. For further information and application forms
contact;
Division of Housing and Food Service
Box 7666
University Station
Austin, TX 78712
Most graduate students stay in the private housing scattered throughout Austin. Although the
cost of such housing varies considerably, typical rentals (not including electricity) are $170-$190
(one-bedroom) and $220-$240 (two-bedroom) for unfurnish»!d apartments; furnished apartments
cost $15-$2O more per month.
Entertainment:
Entertainment in Austin is no problem. The University offers to students who bu\
“Activities Fee” (about $36 per year) a wide variety of cultural and athletic events at little <
cost per event. Plays, concerts, recitals, movies, and lectures by famous personalities are
sponsored by the University and admission is often free. The City of Austin maintains a va
recreational program with many parks and playgrounds. There are excellent munic
swimming pools. Tennis courts and golf courses are located about the city. Two lakes exist wii
the city limits, and six others are scattered up and down the Colorado River within dri\
distance. There are several civic play groups. Many excellent restaurants and numerous ni
clubs for dancing and entertainment can be found in Austin.
Costs for off-campus activities cover a considerable range but prices typically would be
follows; movies, $2-$4.00; plays, $3-5.00; concerts, $4-8.00; and restaurants, $3-10.00- nightclu
$0-2.00 (cover charge), $1.50-2.50 (drinks).
Transportation:
Inter-city bus; Austin is served by a number of regional and national bus companies includi
Greyhound and Trailways.
Intra-city bus:
There is an extensive municipal bus system; the fares are $0.35 at peak commuting hours ar
$0.15 at other times. In addition, UT-Austin operates a shuttle bus service whose routes inclut
those areas of Austin in which there are high concentrations of students. The cost of the shutti
bus is included as part of the required registration fees for all students.
Airlines:
Austin is served by Braniff, Eastern, Continental, Texas International and Southwest Airlines
Automobile titles and licenses:
Out-of-state vehicles should be registered and titled in Texas after establishing residency oi
entering into gainful employment here. How soon this must be done is determined by the
reciprocity agreement between the state of Texas and the state of former residence. Specific
information is available from the Travis County Tax Assessor-Collector’s Title Division
New residents who have a valid driver’s license have 30 days after entry into the state to obtain
a Texas driver’s license. The driving test is not required for applicants who possess a valid license
at the time of application. The fee for a Texas license, valid for four years, is $7.00.
Voting:
To vote in Texas, a person must be a U.S. citizen, must be at least 18 years of age, and possess
a valid voter registration certificate. The latter require a minimum period of 30 days of residency
before the certificate holder is eligible to vote and can be obtained from the Travis Country
Tax-Assessor Collector.
Professional Employment:
Degree holders from the Chemistry department at UT-Austin enter the complete spectrum of
positions available to professional chemists. For example, of the individuals who completed their
degrees during the past five years, approximately 20% are currently in post-doctoral or research
scientist positions in academic or medical school setting and sessional appointments, and 35% are
employed in industry. The remainder are working in government-related laboratories and the like.
Graduates who wish to enter industrial positions are aided in their job-hunting by the
Engineering-Science Career Center, which provides a central clearing-house for prospective
employers and employees to make contact. This center supplies advice about writing resumes,
reproduces them at a nominal cost, and regularly posts announcements of job-openings and
interview schedules for many different companies that are seeking chemists.
There are no geographical boundaries for our graduates in that they find positions throughout
the U.S. as well as abroad.
Fraternal Organizations:
A chapter of Alpha Chi Sigma (professional chemical and chemical engineering fraternity) is
active at the University. Members of this organization will be glad to be of assistance to new
chemistry students; feel free to write to them if you plan to enter the University. Inquiries directed
to this organization can be sent to them in care of the Department of Chemistry.

The University of Texas, with 50,000 students is
the largest university in the Southwest. Some
10,000 graduate students are registered, with
advanced degree programs being offered in all
areas of the sciences and humanities. The gradu￾ate student population comes from all parts of the
nation and around the world.
The campus is located in the center of Austin,
bounded by the state government complex on the
south and by quiet residential areas elsewhere.
Despite the urban surroundings and the large
number of students, a pleasant relaxed atmos￾phere prevails, as suggested by the photographs
on these pages.
The cultural and recreational attractions of the
campus-and the city-extend from dramatic and
musical performances to intercollegiate athletics
contests. Many graduate students are members
of campus organizations, such as fraternal or
religious associations, chess clubs, ethnic clubs,
and so on. Athletics continue to be a principal
recreation of many graduate students, given the
extensive facilities and intramural programs of
the university and the city of Austin.

The Region
Most graduate students live in private rooms
r apartments rather than in university dormito￾es, but beyond this it is impossible to categorize
leir style of living, for the community offers—and
ne graduate students accept—a wide diversity of
fe styles. Old houses close to campus, new
ines on the fringe of town or even out in the
iountry; small apartments in small units down￾bwn; expensive accommodations for students of
ibove-average means or cheap pads for those
vith barely enough to get by; there is housing for
ivery graduate student’s needs.
Just as it is difficult to categorize student hous￾ng, so is it impossible to describe the range of
3ff-campus activities enjoyed by graduate stu￾dents. Some take full advantage of the cultural
offerings available in Austin; others prefer to relax
outdoors or enjoy gourmet dining; many are so
absorbed in their studies that the community
serves only to provide housing and food. Austin
offers a way of life for every taste—and well so,
for most graduate students experience more than
one life style between arrival and departure.
The traditionally limited financial resources of
graduate students somehow—despite inflation,
educational expenses, or perhaps even starting
a family—serve not only to provide the necessi￾ties of food and shelter, but also to sustain what
may be the happiest, most carefree years of
one’s life. It is therefore worth considering
whether the community in which a university is
located will provide the environment that one
wants for his or her graduate school years. Most
Austinites think their city provides the best of
everything any city can offer.
The name “Texas” comes from an Indian word
meaning “friendly,” and this describes Texas, and
Texans, perfectly. The state is so large and varied
that no single description captures the spirit of
every region. See Steinbeck’s Travels with Char￾ley if you wish to read about his impressions and
insights formed while traveling through the state.
The particular part of Texas in which Austin is
located—the Hill Country—is so different from
the desert ranches of the Big Bend country,
the endless expanse of the Panhandle, the
tropical forests of East Texas, and the sandy
beaches of the Gulf Coast that most visitors from
afar are unable to match what they see here with
their cowboy/oil rig/millionaire/longhorn image of
Texas. The countryside is hilly, thickly forested
with oak and cedar, and studded with lakes and
pleasant small towns populated by the descen￾dants of the settlers who came to Texas in the
1800’s. Outdoor recreation is big in central Texas
and graduate students soon acquaint themselves
with activities ranging from water sports to hiking
and caving throughout the Highland Lakes area.
The weather in central Texas is best charac￾terized as semi-tropical, average daily tempera￾ture maxima and minima being as follows;
September-November, 80°-60°; December-Feb￾ruary, 62°-42°; March-May, 75°-55‘’; June-August,
93°-72°. Snow and ice are rare visitors to the
area, coming only about once a year and surviv￾ing no more than a day or two. Rainfall is plentiful,
averaging 36" per year, and the vegetation is lush
and green as a result, in sharp contrast with the
desert-like regions of West Texas.

Research Specializations
The Department of Chemistry is loosely organized into five divisions according to research field.
Graduate students usually decide upon their division of primary research interest before entering
graduate school, or shortly thereafter, and in the course of their first year associate themselves
with a supervising professor with whom their M.A. or Ph.D. research is done. Each division is
responsible for counseling first-year graduate students within the division and administering the
course and major examination requirements for its own students.
A further divisional responsibility integral to the training of our graduate students is organization
of a weekly research seminar program that includes presentations by chemists from laboratories
throughout the world, as well as by graduate students and post-doctoral fellows. In addition to
these seminars, the department annually sponsors a Distinguished Visiting Lecturer series in which
a number of eminent scientists spend one to two weeks in Austin presenting formal lectures on
the status of their research and interacting informally with faculty and graduate students. Some
recent participants in this program include D. Merschbach (Harvard), S. Masamune (MIT), M. Eigen
(Max Planck Institute), D. Barton (Imperial College), T. Brown (Illinois), N. Turro (Columbia), J.
Berson (Yale), S. Rice (Chicago), W. Klemperer (Harvard), O. Chapman (UCLA), D. Lemal (Dart￾mouth), E. Van Tamelen (Stanford), G. Pimental (Berkeley), R. Hoffmann (Cornell), F. Cotton
(Texas A&M), H. Taube (Stanford), J. D. Dunitz (Zurich), T. Marks (Northwestern), G. M. Whitesides
(MIT), H. Gerischer (Max Planck Inst.), F. G. A. Stone (Bristol, England), J. Sinfelt (Exxon), C. B.
Harris (Berkeley), C. H. Heathcock (Berkeley), R. Murray (North Carolina), Y Kishi (Harvard), R.
J. Madix (Stanford), H. Kagan (Paris), H. Gray (Caltech), R. Grubbs (Caltech), R. Bergman (Berke￾ley), and G. Stork (Columbia). These seminars and extended visits are outstanding opportunities
for young scientists to develop in-depth knowledge of the frontiers of research in chemistry, to
make valuable personal contacts, and to receive stimulation for the development of their own
programs.
On the following pages are presented summaries of the general degree requirements of each
division and brief description of the research activities of the individual faculty members. The latter
should assist you in determining whether or not a program fitted to your particular interests is
available in our department.
These descriptions should also assist you when the time comes to select a research supervisor.
The department encourages its students to make this important decision as early as possible, and
facilitates the process by offering informal seminars during the Fall semester in which the faculty
discuss their areas of research. This initial exposure is then augmented by the graduate student
meeting individually with the faculty in the student’s division of specialization. Normally, most stu￾dents have joined a particular research group by the end of their first semester of residence.
Further information about the research programs of any of the groups can be obtained from the
individual professors.

Thomas E. Mallouk
Our research program is concerned primarily
with the preparation, structure, electronic and
electrochemical properties of solid state com￾pounds. Of particular interest to us are interca￾lation reactions, i.e., those which occur with the
motion of molecular species into a solid without
gross structural reorganization of the host lat￾tice. In general, these reactions proceed with
some degree of charge transfer, and so may be
driven either chemically or electrochemically.
We are currently investigating the oxidative in￾tercalation of graphite and other lamellar sub￾stances. Compounds produced in this way
(fluorides, hydroxides, sulfonates, and phos￾phonates) are themselves powerful oxidants
and good electronic and ionic conductors. X-ray
diffraction is a powerful tool in characterizing
these materials, but because they are usually
disordered, it rarely provides a complete picture
of local bonding environments. To this end a va￾riety of physical methods are applied, including
vibrational spectroscopy, NMR, photoelectron
spectroscopy, magnetic, and electrochemical
measurements. Another interesting group of in￾tercalation compounds is produced by the re￾action of lithium with layered or framework
hosts. We are exploring the reactions of lithiat￾ing agents with intermetallics, with an eye to
preparing compounds that lie near Li metal in
the electrochemical series; such compounds
could replace the lithium electrode in non￾aqueous secondary batteries.
The thermodynamic stability of intercalation
compounds and their position in the electro￾chemical series are sensitive functions of elec￾tron and ion affinities, lattice energies, and
solvation free energies. Electrochemical meas￾urements, lattice energy calculations, and direct
measurement of reaction energetics are under￾way. The aim is to understand the stabilization
of unusual complex ions and the energetic im￾portance of solvent interactions within the host
lattice. A long-range goal is to develop calcula￾tions of sufficiently high quality to allow predic￾tions of the stability of unknown compounds and
to guide new syntheses.
Another active research area involves the
chemical modification of electrode surfaces to
produce organized sub-micron structures. Our
current effort is concentrated on two such sys￾tems, each possessing a high degree of molec￾ular order. These are the zeolites and transition
metal phosphates. The former are framework
aluminosilicates which contain cavities and tun￾nels of adjustable size and exchangeable cat￾ions. The latter are lamellar compounds of
adjustable layer spacing which may be built up
from the surface in the manner of Langmuir￾Blodgett multilayer films. We are concerned with
electron transfer, molecular diffusion, electro￾catalysis, and light-driven charge separation in
these organized systems.
We are at present synthesizing and investi￾gating the electronic properties of new low￾dimensional conducting polymers; these poly￾mers contain inorganic building blocks such as
mefalloporphyrins and phthalocyanines. One
goal of this research is to structurally tailor these
polymers to show conductivity modulation when
small molecule analytes, such as gas-phase CO
or Oj, bind to the metal.

Dean Ramsay Appling
Dr. Appling's research interests center on two
fundamental biological questions. The first is
concerned with the mechanisms of various reg￾ulatory processes. All organisms, from “simple”
single-cell bacteria to complex multicellular eu￾karyotes, possess precise regulatory processes
in which some signal, carrying information about
the state of the environment, is translated into
an appropriate compensating action. These
processes include control of the rates and direc￾tion of metabolic pathways within cells, hor￾monal and neuronal transfer of information
between cells, and even chemical communica￾tion between individual organisms, as exempli￾fied by pheromones. Work currently in progress
is aimed at characterizing the regulation of fol￾ate-mediated one-carbon metabolism in mam￾mals. This complex pathway is involved in the
biosynthesis of DNA and protein precursors and
is thus central to intermediary metabolism. The
interconversion of various forms of the folate
coenzymes must be controlled very tightly to in￾sure that the immediate biosynthetic needs of
the cell are met with a limited supply of cofactor.
The ultimate goal of this work is to identify the
signal(s) responsible for the regulation and to
elucidate the mechanisms by which information
is transferred. These questions are being ap￾proached from a number of directions, including
assays of enzyme activity and concentration, as
well as examination of gene expression at the
level of transcription by measurement of mRNA
levels through the use of the powerful tech￾niques of molecular biology.
Dr. Appling's second area of interest in￾volves structure-function relationships in pro￾teins. The translation of a three-dimensional
structure into a specific function is the underly￾ing principle of biological organization. Multi￾functional proteins, i.e. proteins which possess
multiple biological activities within a single poly￾peptide chain, are particularly interesting model
systems. A trifunctional enzyme which cata￾lyzes three reactions responsible for the inter￾conversion of folate cofactors has been purified
from yeast and is being characterized. The in￾teraction of domains of the protein and active
site relationships are being studied by a variety
of techniques including protein chemistry, im￾munochemistry, and site-directed mutagenesis
of the cloned gene which codes for the enzyme.
Future studies will focus on this and other mul￾tifunctional enzymes from mammals.

Phenylketonuria. The genetic disease phenylk￾etonuria (PKU) is characterized by high levels

either the high phenylalanine levels, the high

IV. Immobilized Enzyme Based CO? Scrubbers
for Underwater Systems. For deep sea diving
and for submersible vehicles the disposal of
gaseous COj from expired air or from the ex￾haust of an engine poses considerable prob￾lems. For underwater breathing the depth and
length of a dive is limited by the amount of CO2

’rofessor Mosbaugh's research interest has fo￾cused on understanding the fundamental bio-
