apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease, exPnu￾clease, DNA polymerse and DNA ligase) in￾volved in the base excision-repair pathway are
being investigated. By studying the mecha￾nisms and specificities of these enzymes, we

DNA repair. In addition, we are interested in

lesions formed by specific chemical agents
which damage DNA.

Yale University. Organic Chemistry; Reactive in￾termediates; reaction mechanisms; pericyclic
phenomena; synthetic methods.
John Carl Gilbert
Professor Gilbert and his research group are
engaged in studies whose objectives range
from the theoretical and experimental under￾standing of various types of problems of impor￾tance in physical organic chemistry to the
development of approaches to the total synthe￾sis of biologically active natural products.
Among the studies currently being pursued
in the former category are the generation and
chemistry of novel diazocompounds and the
carbenes derived from them. Of particular inter￾est to us are the alkylidene and alkenylidene
carbenes, unsaturated entities that possess fas￾cinating electronic and chemical properties and
have provided a wealth of rewarding research
problems for our group. We have been able to
develop a novel approach to the synthesis of
cyclopentyne by way of cyclobutylidenecar￾bene, for example, and have been successful in
unveiling some novel chemistry of this highly
strained alkyne as a result. Attempts to correlate
the experimental observations we have made
with theoretically predicted properties of the cy￾cloalkyne are presently underway. Similar com￾binations of theoretical and experimental
studies are being executed to define the nature
of these fascinating types of unsaturated car￾benes.
Another program of research that falls under
the broad aegis of physical organic chemistry
involves study of a variety of pericyclic phenom￾ena. Of particular interest at the present time
are [3.3]-sigmatropic reactions. Our interests
here reside mainly in defining various stereo￾chemical aspects of such processes and in elu￾cidating the nature of catalytic and electronic
modifications that can result in enormous rate
accelerations for the reactions. It is expected
that what is learned from the mechanistic stud￾ies will ultimately prove of substantial impor￾tance not only to the theory of such pericyclic
reactions but also to the design of syntheses.
Within the category of organic synthesis,
considerable effort is presently being invested
in the development of highly convergent ap￾proaches to the trichothecenes, a class of ses￾quiterpenes some members of which exhibit
potent biological activity. The natural products
themselves are desired synthetic targets, as are
various structural analogs of them; it is hoped
that the latter will have even greater pharma￾cological activities of potential benefit. Another
line of synthetic research is the evaluation of
novel methods for the synthesis of various types
of cyclopentanoids, including the pyrrolizidines,
which are alkaloids that constitute an important
class of biologically significant molecules.

Evan Peter Kyba
Currently, Professor Kyba's major research in￾terests lie in the area of modification of proper￾ties of transition metals (TM) as a function of the
coordinated ligands. The short-term goal is to
develop new chemistry of TM complexes and
the long-term goal is to apply this new knowl￾edge to the development of novel catalysts for
organic reactions. Toward this end, the synthe￾sis and study of macrocyclic polyphosphines
and polyheteropolyphosphines is being actively
pursued. Such molecules are extremely good
complexing agents of transition metals. Valua￾ble results are being realized in the study of: (a)
unusual valence levels of transition metals; (b)
catalytic properties of various macrocyclic li￾gand-transition metal complexes in a variety of
organic reactions, particularly with a view to new
catalytic systems; (c) selective sequestering of
transition metal ions by “custom-built" macro￾cyclic ligand systems. Chiral tricoordinating
phosphine and arsine ligands are being devel￾oped in order to maximize asymmetric induction
in the transition metal catalysis of organic reac￾tions involving prochiral substrates.
In the past ten years there has been a tre￾mendous wave of research effort in the area of
TM clusters, which have great potential as ca￾talysts tor a wide variety of reactions. A major
problem has been the maintenance of metal￾metal bonds, that is, cluster integrity. Professor
Kyba's approach to the enhancement of cluster
stability is to utilize linked bis(bridging) phos￾phide ligands, which his group has shown does
enhance cluster stability as well as generating
new chemistry of such systems. Current inves￾tigations involve the syntheses of new clusters
and the study of the organometallic mechanistic
and synthetic chemistry of these species.

Professor Roberts' main research interests lie
in the area of Friedel-Crafts chemistry. In 1877
the French chemist Charles Friedel and the
American chemist James M. Crafts first de￾scribed the results of their collaborative investi￾gations on the action of aluminum chloride on
organic compounds. Since that time the reac￾tions which bear their names have grown to en￾compass a wide area of organic chemistry.
Although the Friedel-Crafts alkylation reac￾tion has been widely used as a synthetic pro￾cedure (millions of pounds of styrene and
cumene are produced annually), there are in￾herent limitations which have complicated its
practical applications. One of the most severe
has been the possible rearrangement of the al￾kyl group whenever an alkylbenzene with a side
chain longer than ethyl is to be synthesized.
This problem could not be studied successfully
until modern instrumentation became available
in the 195O’s. Much light has been thrown on
this problem by Professor Roberts' research in
the last two decades, and a new type of molec￾ular rearrangement was discovered through the
use of carbon-14 as radioactive label. It involves
rearrangement of a sidechain after attachment
to the aromatic ring. This new rearrangement
has been called "the alkylbenzene rearrange￾ment."
In view of the widespread current interest in
coal as an energy source, and the fact that
some of the first significant structural informa￾tion on coal was provided by a Friedel-Crafts
type reaction, basic research on coal has been
undertaken. This work has so far included at￾tempts to transalkylate fragments from coal ma￾cromolecules to simpler aromatic molecules
using Friedel-Crafts catalysts, with the aim of
depolymerizing coal, and studies on ozonation
as a means of identifying the aliphatic compo￾nents of coal.
Recently attention has been turned to cer￾tain novel reactions of hindered aromatic
ketones and sulfones in the presence of Friedel￾Crafts catalysts.

Jonathan Lawrence Sessler
My group might be considered to be in the busi￾ness of “Molecular Engineering" in that our re￾search involves the design and construction of
molecules carefully tailored so as to accomplish
a specific objective. These objectives are often
“bio-inspired". In such cases, we seek to un￾derstand complex biochemical processes
through the study of simple, well-characterized
"model" compounds. With these, we seek to re￾produce the essential structural and/or pheno￾menalogical features of an elaborate natural
system. Frequently, however, we try to prove in￾teresting physical phenomena and exploit any
new knowledge we acquire. This work involves
not just organic synthesis but also detailed
spectroscopic and physical studies. As a result
the research projects are often highly interdis￾ciplinary in nature. The chemistry involves at
times elements of classic organometallic, or in￾organic coordination chemistry, as well as more
novel complexation studies.
One area of investigation is concerned with
developing chemical analogues of the active
site of hemerythrin. Hemerythrin is the protein
which serves to bind and transport oxygen in a
variety of worms. In contrast to hemoglobin,
hemerythrin does not contain a porphyrin pros￾thetic group. Rather the active site of hemery￾thrin contains a special diiron(ll) center. It is not
currently known why this type of oxygen carrier
evolved or how precisely it functions at the mo￾lecular level. By synthesizing small, well-char￾acterized “model" diiron(ll) complexes we may
be in a position to help biochemists answer
these questions.
A portion of our research concerns further
exploring further aspects of the chemistry of
metalloporphyrins and related compounds. The
impetus for this research stems from the fact
that porphyrin and porphyrin-like compounds
are found at the active sites of a large number
of enzymes and metalloproteins. Porphyrin
complexes are also proving to be highly active
as synthetic catalysts. One goal of our work in
this area is the development of improved cata￾lysts for the reductive activation of small mole￾cules such as O2 and COj. A second goal
involves developing large macrocyclic com￾pounds which should form stable, porphyrin-like
complexes with lanthanide and actinide cations.
This will provide a new way of exploring the co￾ordination chemistry and catalytic properties of
the post-transition metals.
We are also working to develop new classes
of binucleating ligands. Two kinds of complexes
are being considered. The first are homobinu￾clear. They are of interest as templates for ef￾fecting controlled organic syntheses. For
instance, the organometallic chemistry of cobalt
is being exploited as a means of binding and
activating for inter-reaction two alkyl-containing
substrates. This approach is being explored as
a means of synthesizing large ring compounds
such as muscone. The second kind of com￾plexes are heterobinuclear. These are particu￾larly interesting in the case where two widely
differing species are bound in close proximity.
Experimental studies will give valuable insight
into the nature of metal-metal interactions.
These studies may lead to the development of
a new class of analytical detection devices.
We are also intrigued by the possibility of
constructing “molecular cages" whereby a
small organic molecule could be completely
trapped within a larger discreet molecular struc￾ture. This challenging project requires the con￾struction of a framework which not only serves
as a surrounding “host" for the binding of a
smaller “guest" but also structurally incorpo￾rates a “door" which could be covalently closed
after the “guest" is bound.

Craig Wilcox
The synthesis of structurally elaborate organic
molecules presents an exciting challenge to the
organic chemist. This challenge stimulates the
discovery of efficient new processes for bond
formation and illuminates new unifying concepts
of molecular reactivity. There are many possible
goals for a project in organic synthesis. While
the synthesis of biologically active natural prod￾ucts is often of immediate importance to the
pharmaceutical industry and to the biochemical
and medical sciences, of equal interest is the
design and synthesis of “unnatural” molecules.
These molecules are often required to test cur￾rent physical organic or bioorganic hypotheses,
and the design, preparation, and testing of such
molecules can be as rewarding as is the synthe￾sis of a natural product.
Biomimetic chemistry is an exciting and ac￾tive research discipline wherein the organic
chemist attempts design relatively simple sys￾tems that imitate molecular events which occur
in living organisms. We are interested in syn￾thesizing molecules which mimic a commonly
observed biological phenomenon bimolecular
complexation. The ability of biomolecules to
"recognize” one another through non-covalent
binding interactions is a fundamental aspect of
many important cellular events. Enzymic catal￾ysis, allosteric effects, drug receptors, ion trans￾port, molecular transport, antibody-antigen
recognition, and nucleic acid replication all in￾volve highly ordered molecular complexes.
Molecules may bind to each other through elec￾trostatic effects, hydrophobic forces, van der
Waals attraction, hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole
interactions and solvent liberation driving
forces. The goal of this program is to design and
synthesize relatively simple molecules which
will associate and form bimolecular complexes.
Models will be sought which will allow quantita￾tive predictions of binding phenomena. These
studies will lead to a more detailed understand￾ing of the forces which result in the formation of
bimolecular complexes of specific configuration.
In a more traditional application of synthetic
chemistry, research is underway in several
areas related to the total synthesis of biologi￾cally active natural products. The goal of these
studies is to evolve practical methods for the
synthesis of complex molecules and to enrich
our understanding of chemical reactions. Be￾cause of the entropic advantages and stereo￾chemical control inherent in intramolecular
reactions, special emphasis is being given to
the discovery and refinement of new techniques
for intramolecular bond formation.
Many molecules of pharmaceutical interest,
including rationally designed drugs, enzyme in￾hibitors, and naturally occurring substances of
diverse biological activity, contain polyhy￾droxylated carbocyclic rings. We are exploring
an efficient and economical approach to the
synthesis of such systems which is based on
the cyclization of radicals derived from unsatu￾rated halo-sugars. In another area, the synthe￾sis of citreoviridin, a heterocyclic mycotoxin,
was recently completed and work is now di￾rected toward other polyoxygenated hetero￾cyclic acetogenins and terpenes.
The use of steric interactions, stereoelec￾tronic effects, and intramolecular complexation
for the control of conformation and electrophilic/
nucleophilic reactivity is a theme present
throughout our program. Through these studies
we hope to gain valuable insights into the fac￾tors which control organic reactions and molec￾ular interactions. Knowledge gained in these
studies will be practically applicable in any ef￾forts in which organic molecules, the elements
of life, are under investigation.

Graduate students interested in physical chemistry will
find among sixteen research groups at Texas a diversity
of experimental and theoretical problems from which to
choose a research field. All of the physical chemistry
groups now occupy spacious new laboratories in Welch
Hall.
Experimental research within the division emphasizes
the following areas: kinetics of gas phase and surface
reactions, gas phase and solid phase photochemical and
photophysical processes, interfacial phenomena, physi￾cal properties of macromolecular systems, and structural
and dynamical studies employing x-ray and electron dif￾fraction, ESR/NMR spectroscopy, and surface spectros￾copy. Each of the experimental groups maintains its own
laboratory facilities; in addition, the department maintains
a strong group of major instruments including mass, Ra￾man, infrared, ultraviolet, nuclear magnetic resonance
and electron spin resonance spectrometers, and com￾puter controlled x-ray diffractometers. The experimental
research is also supported by eleven staff members in
the glassblowing, electronics, and machine shops.
A strong program in theoretical chemistry is provided
by the six faculty research groups in the Institute for The￾oretical Chemistry. About 45 graduate students and post￾doctoral fellows conduct research in the following areas:
ab initio electronic structure calculations on small and me￾dium-sized molecules, semi-empirical calculations on
large organic molecules, group theoretic approaches to
electronic structure problems, the statistical mechanics of
liquids, energy transport in solids, and the dynamics of
chemical reactions and laser-molecule interactions.
The University computation center, one of the finest
facilities in the country (with dual CDC CYBER 170/750,
IBM 3081 -D and DEC-20 systems and an advanced com￾puter graphics laboratory), is heavily used in both theo￾retical and experimental research done at Texas. This
facility is accessed through numerous remote terminals
in Welch Hall, and at several batch processing centers
adjacent to Welch Hall. This strength in computational
facilities will be greatly enhanced when a major new
mainframe computer is installed within the next year.
Students begin work in physical chemistry by taking
two divisional qualifying courses during their first year.
These courses are at the top of the listing below, along
with some of the courses available to students pursuing
graduate degrees in physical chemistry.
383M-Quantum Chemistry (qualifier)
382L-Statistical Thermodynamics (qualifier)
382J-Survey of Physical Chemistry
393L-Photophysics and Photochemistry
393L-Molecular Structure
393L-lnterfacial Phenomena
393L-Reaction Kinetics
Students taking degrees in physical chemistry must take
both of the qualifying courses in addition to qualifying
courses in two other areas of chemistry — organic, inor￾ganic, analytical or biochemistry. Students in chemical
physics take only one qualifying course besides the two
physical chemistry courses mentioned previously. In
addition, they take an advanced course in quantum
mechanics, and several courses in physics and mathe￾matics.
During the latter part of their first semester, students
are expected to select a research supervisor. Course
work, other than described above, is determined by the
student in consultation with his or her supervising profes￾sor and a committee appointed by the graduate dean.
During their third semester, students in physical chemistry
and chemical physics desiring the Ph.D. degree are re￾quired to prepare and orally defend two research propos￾als on topics in physical chemistry of their choosing,
subject to the restriction that the proposals must be from
diverse areas of physical chemistry.
The division of physical chemistry maintains a weekly
seminar program for students and faculty with speakers
from other institutions. In addition, there are many visitors
to the individual research groups, providing lively contacts
with researchers elsewhere in this country and abroad.

Entrance and Degree Requirements
The preliminary training of students wishing to major in chemistry for a graduate
degree must include a minimum of twenty-four semester hours in chemistry, of
which twelve or more must be of at least upper-division (junior and senior level)
courses. Within the twenty-four hours, there should have been two semester
courses in organic chemistry (including laboratory) and two in physical chemistry;
one in analytical chemistry; and one in inorganic chemistry. Applicants lacking the
prescribed background may still be admitted, but will be required to rectify any
such deficiencies with appropriate coursework.
For entrance into the Graduate School, an applicant normally must:
(1) hold a bachelor’s degree from an accredited institution in the U.S. or have
had equivalent training in a foreign university;
(2) have a 3.0 GPA in upper division work and any graduate work already
completed;
(3) score at least 1000 on the Graduate Record Examination Aptitude Test;
(4) GRE Advanced Test in Chemistry is mandatory for all foreign applicants;
(5) Foreign applicants must score at least 550 on the Test of English as a
Foreign Language Examination (TOEFL).
The admissions committee of the Department of Chemistry strongly recom￾mends, but does not require, that all applicants submit scores from the Advanced
Chemistry Test of the Graduate Record Examination. This is particularly important
for applicants wishing to be considered for fellowship support.
The chemistry faculty believes that teaching experience is an essential part of
the education of graduate students, and therefore requires each degree candidate
to teach, usually by taking charge of laboratory work in undergraduate courses for
a minimum of two semesters. The Graduate School recognizes the value of this
experience by awarding three semester hours of credit (which may be applied
toward a graduate degree) for a maximum of two semesters of registration in
Chemistry 398T, Supervised Teaching for Graduate Students.
Master of Arts The Master of Arts degree is based on satisfactory completion
of thirty semester hours of work, of which the thesis (which is mandatory) counts
for six semester hours. From six to twelve hours of the course work normally must
be taken in an outside, but closely allied, graduate area (usually mathematics,
physics, biological sciences, geological sciences, pharmacy, or chemical engi￾neering, but occasionally others, such as education). Up to nine hours of work, of
upper-division rank, but not more than six hours in either the major or the minor,
may be counted in the program; the balance must be in courses of graduate rank.
The submission of a thesis based upon independent scientific research is an
integral component of this degree.
Doctor of Philosophy Many graduate students in chemistry work directly to￾ward the Ph.D. degree without the M.A. degree as an intermediate objective.
Advanced course work is an integral part of the doctoral candidates program;
however, there is no set minimum number of semester hours required for the
degree. The Ph.D. degree is awarded on the basis of the candidate’s demonstra￾tion of mastery of the selected field and of his/her ability for independent scholar￾ship and research in it. In addition to taking the qualifying coursework in the major

Time required for degree:
The period of time required to complete a graduate degree is variable, but some
generalizations are meaningful. For example, it is difficult for an individual to com￾plete the coursework and research associated with a Master of Arts degree in less
than one and one-half years. Most students, however can finish this degree in two
years.
A few individuals complete the Ph.D. degree in as little as three years. More
commonly, an average of four to five and one-half years is needed to earn the
degree, with the final three years of this period involving research work almost
exclusively.

record in undergraduate and, if applicable, previous graduate work, letters of rec￾ommendation, general promise of successful pursuit of graduate study, and ac￾ceptance for admission to the Graduate School. Stipends range upward from
